ra.title: REMOTE ACCESS
ra.sub: Open Javis from your phone or another computer over HTTPS, no VPS needed.
ra.intro_long: Javis downloads and runs cloudflared (Cloudflare's official free tool) right on this computer. That way a Windows or macOS machine at home can be opened from anywhere over HTTPS, with the microphone and voice working. No router port to open, no static IP and no VPS. When the computer is off or asleep, the link is down too. A login password is required: if the password is removed, the tunnel stops right away.

ra.step1: Go to one.dash.cloudflare.com, Networks, Tunnels, click Create a tunnel, pick Cloudflared and give it a name.
ra.step2: On the connector install step, copy the command (Windows or Mac, either works) and paste it in the box below. You do not need to run it.
ra.step3: On the Public Hostname step: pick your domain (it must use Cloudflare DNS), set Service to HTTP and put the service address below in the URL box.
ra.step4: Come back and click Turn on. Your fixed link is https:// plus the domain you picked.

ol.dk_title: Three steps, on the SERVER itself, not in Javis's terminal
ol.dk_b1: SSH into the VPS as root. Javis's own terminal will not do: it runs inside the container, has no root, and anything installed there is wiped on the next update.
ol.dk_b3: Make Ollama listen on the Docker bridge address. Only containers on this host can reach it and nothing is exposed to the Internet, so no firewall step is needed:
ol.dk_b4: The address is already filled in below - just press Connect:
ol.dk_canh_bao: The command above binds Ollama to an internal address, so no firewall is needed. Only if you must use OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 (unusual Docker network) does Ollama listen to the whole Internet, and it has NO password: run ufw allow from THE-BRIDGE-SUBNET to any port 11434 then ufw deny 11434, or block port 11434 in your VPS provider's firewall.
ol.dk_cham: A VPS usually has no GPU and little RAM, so a CPU-bound model will be very slow. Your desktop at home (with a GPU, ideally) is the better host, at the cost of the VPS having to reach it.
ol.dk_khong_do_duoc: Javis could not work out the host address. Run the command below on the host, then put the number that follows the word default into the box above, with :11434 after it.
ol.dk_chan_doan: Still not connecting? On the host run: ss -ltnp | grep 11434. No line means Ollama is not running (see systemctl status ollama). A line with 127.0.0.1 means step 3 has not been done.

rp.auto_note: The bot weighs each group message on its own, with nothing to configure: it works out who is being addressed, reads the last few messages and checks them against the Agent's role and the bot's documents. It learns as it goes from how the group reacts and from your Right/Wrong buttons (the "..." menu on the bot card, Reply judge). To learn, it keeps the group's chat text: up to 400 characters per message for 14 days, and learned cases for 180 days. Forget all wipes it. In private 1-1 chats the bot's own Agent chooses to reply, stay silent, or stay silent and alert you in the bell on a hard question; private chats are not in the statistics and are not learned from.

lv.intro_what: Sign in once in your own browser, then hand that session to Javis: it can read pages behind the sign-in and watch pages strangers cannot see.
lv.intro_s1: Install the Cookie-Editor extension for Chrome or Edge.
lv.intro_s2: Open the site while signed in (for example your Shopee seller page), click the Cookie-Editor icon, choose Export then JSON.
lv.intro_s3: Press Add cookies here and paste it. If you saved it as a file, press Upload file.
lv.intro_formats: Javis also reads a cookies.txt file (for example from the Get cookies.txt LOCALLY extension), a JSON file and a name=value; ... string.
lv.intro_safe: Cookies are encrypted on the server. Only someone signed in to the dashboard can add sign-ins or see the list. The AI never sees a cookie value, only the page text. Customer chatbots cannot use this vault.
lv.intro_note: A cookie is a key to the account, so never paste someone else's. Facebook and Google often ask to verify when a session is used from another IP (such as a VPS). If a site has an official API or MCP, prefer that. Javis only reads pages; it does not click buttons or send forms.

msc.intro: Connect a Facebook Page so a bot answers its Messenger inbox and the comments under its posts. Create a Meta app once, paste the App ID and App secret, click Log in with Facebook and tick the Pages to connect. Javis gets a non-expiring Page token, registers the webhook, subscribes the Page to the app and checks every step. Once connected, open Chatbot, Bots to create a bot for this channel.
msc.form_head: Connect a Facebook Page to Messenger
msc.form_how: Do this on Meta first: create an app with the Messenger use case and connect the Page in Messenger API settings. Token: open Graph API Explorer, pick the right app, add pages_show_list, pages_messaging, pages_manage_metadata, pages_read_engagement, click Generate Access Token and tick the right Page. A short-lived token is fine, Javis converts it.

improve.procedure_hint: Add a working procedure (planning, source checks, output checks, handoff format) to one assistant's prompt, only where you tick. The assistant file, memory, your rules, model and permissions are not changed. Javis refuses text that sets model, permissions or skills, contains JAVIS_ markers, or says to ignore your rules. A private chat already in progress keeps the old prompt; new chats use the procedure. If you edit your rules or the assistant file, the procedure pauses until you apply it again.

improve.auto_hint: Javis reviews the chat turns that used a skill, an assistant or a workflow. When the same mistake shows up at least three times, it writes its own test questions, revises the instructions, compares with the current version and keeps the new one only when it is clearly better and breaks nothing the current version got right. Everything follows the Learning page: turning on Learning plus Skill, Role and Step chain is all it takes, nothing else to do. In Auto-write mode Javis applies the change itself, in Suggest mode it waits for you to press Apply, in Dry run it only records mistakes. At most one change a day, on the brain you selected, with no tools; the old version is always kept for undo.

improve.loop_hint: Javis uses examples with answers in skills/SKILL-NAME/examples.json (each with prompt, expected and an optional family; you can ask Javis to write this file in chat). About a quarter are used for trying, the rest stay sealed for the verdict; examples that already judged an earlier version move to the trying side. Javis edits only the skill body, proposes fixes from two angles, test-runs them, combines what works, then compares with the current skill on the sealed part, twice per question. It runs on the brain you selected (Claude Code, Codex or an API brain), nothing to install. The skill only changes when you press Apply, and the old version is kept in Javis's data folder.

gh.intro: GitHub is built into Javis, nothing to install. Connect once (press Sign in with GitHub, or paste a token), then in a chat press plus and pick GitHub repo to attach repos to the conversation. Javis downloads the repo to this machine (outside the brain folder), and each conversation works on its own branch and folder, so two chats never overwrite each other.
gh.missing_scopes: The token is missing scopes: {scopes}. Reading works, but Javis needs them to push code.
gh.no_git: git is not installed on this machine, so repos cannot be downloaded yet.
gh.local_how: Removing from the brain deletes only the copy on this machine; the repo on GitHub stays as it is. Javis refuses while there are unsaved edits or commits not pushed yet, so no work is lost.

gh.token_how: On github.com go to Settings, Developer settings, Personal access tokens, Fine-grained tokens, Generate new token. Pick the repos Javis may work on and grant: Contents (Read and write), Pull requests (Read and write), Workflows (Read and write), Checks, Actions, Commit statuses and Metadata (Read). Paste the github_pat_... string here. A classic token (ghp_...) needs the repo and workflow scopes.
gh.signin_sub: No token to make. You choose which repos Javis can see.
gh.signin_how: Javis uses a GitHub App called Javis OS. Press the button and Javis shows a short code. Open the GitHub page, paste the code and press Authorize; there is no token to make or copy. Then install the app on the repos you want Javis to work on; a repo without it stays invisible to Javis. The app only asks for Contents, Pull requests, Workflows (read and write) and Checks, Commit statuses, Actions (read only). It works on a VPS with no browser too. To revoke it, go to GitHub, Settings, Applications.
gh.code_how: Press Open GitHub, paste this code on that page, then press Authorize.

gh.checks_how: After every turn that changes code, Javis runs these commands in the chat's working folder, before pushing to GitHub. If one fails, nothing is pushed. The first time Javis reads them from the repo's CI (.github/workflows) and package.json, leaving out steps that install into the machine, need secrets or deploy. End a line with a backslash to continue a long command. A command that cannot run because a tool is missing counts as skipped, and CI decides.
gh.checks_suggested: Using the list Javis read from the repo's CI.
gh.checks_reset: Use the list read from CI

gh.queue_head: Next jobs, run once the PR is merged
gh.metrics_how: Every merged job records the engine and model that wrote it, whether CI was green on the first push, how many fix rounds it took, how many issues the cross review caught and how long it took. After a few dozen jobs this table shows which model fits this repo, in real numbers.
